opus-5.5.text:
I think for kids of my generation in China, the internet arrived at a very particular moment. Before it, your world was quite small: your school, your teachers, your parents, maybe a few books you could get your hands on. What you learned was mostly what was put in front of you.

When the internet came, the biggest change for me wasn't really information, although that mattered. It was that I suddenly had a way to find people who cared about the same strange things I cared about. There were forums, bulletin boards, little communities where you could ask a question about programming or games or some random technical thing, and someone you'd never met would answer seriously. That was quite shocking as a kid. Nobody there knew how old you were or what your grades were. If what you said was interesting, people engaged with it.

That changed how I thought about expressing myself. In school, expression was mostly about getting the right answer, the answer the teacher expected. Online it was more like you put an idea out there, people pushed back, you argued, and sometimes you were wrong, which was fine. I think that was my first real experience of what an open intellectual community feels like, and in a way it's not so different from what I like about research now. You share something half-formed, others build on it or tear it apart, and the whole thing moves forward.

It also made learning feel self-directed. You didn't have to wait for someone to decide you were ready for a topic. If you were curious, you could just go find it, follow one link to another, and spend the whole night falling down a rabbit hole. Looking back, I think that habit of following curiosity wherever it leads, without asking permission, really started then.

r001.rationale: The response says the internet let him put ideas out in forums, argue with others, and express himself beyond passively receiving what school or adults presented.

fable-5.1.text:
I grew up in Jinan, in Shandong, and I was a pretty ordinary kid in the sense that my world was basically school, home, and whatever books happened to be in the house. Then around the late nineties, when I was maybe in middle school, we got a dial-up connection. I still remember the sound of the modem. And honestly, it felt like someone had knocked a hole in the wall of a room I didn't even know was a room.

Before that, if you wanted to know something, you asked a teacher or you went to find a book, and the book was usually a translation that was ten years old. After that, I could suddenly read what people were saying right now, in other countries, about things no one around me cared about. I spent a lot of time on BBS forums, on Tianya, later on some technical forums. I was reading about computers, about programming, about music. A lot of it I only half understood, but the half-understanding was the exciting part. It taught me that knowledge wasn't something you were handed in order. You could just wander into it.

The other thing, and I think this is actually more important for me, is that it changed how I expressed myself. I was a fairly quiet kid in person. I wasn't the one raising my hand. But online, in text, I could take my time, I could write something carefully, post it, and strangers would respond to the idea rather than to me. Nobody knew I was fourteen. That was very liberating. I learned to argue, to write, to be wrong in public and survive it. Looking back, that's not so different from what research is. You put something out, people push on it, and you revise.

So I would say the internet didn't make me smarter exactly, but it made me curious in a less obedient way, and it gave me a voice earlier than the offline world would have. Both of those stayed with me.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts earlier learning through teachers and books with posting carefully written ideas online, where strangers responded. This clearly conveys a shift from consuming information to publicly expressing his views.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change was that learning became much more self-directed. Before, what you could learn depended largely on your textbooks, your teachers, and the people around you. With the internet, you could follow your curiosity—you’d encounter something interesting, search for it, and discover a whole set of questions you hadn’t thought to ask.

It also expanded the audience you could express yourself to. You weren’t limited to classmates or people who already knew you. You could find people with similar interests, share an idea, and get a response. That made learning and expression feel connected: you learned something, tried to explain it, and then realized through the conversation what you didn’t yet understand.

r001.rationale: The response says the internet let him share ideas with a wider audience and get responses, but it does not clearly describe a shift from one-way information consumption to publicly expressing his own views.

sol-6.1.text:
The internet made my world feel much bigger. Before that, learning was largely about what was in your textbooks and what the teacher told you. Online, you could follow your own curiosity—one question could lead to another, and suddenly you were exploring something that had nothing to do with school.

It also gave me another way to express myself. As a child, you don’t necessarily have many people around you who share your interests. On the internet, you could find those people, share something you’d made or an idea you had, and get a response. That feeling—that you could both learn from the world and contribute something to it—was really exciting.

r001.rationale: The response says the internet let him share something he made or an idea and receive a response, but it does not clearly describe a shift from one-way information consumption to publicly expressing his own views.
